identity.title: Verifying Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Its Computational Graph

problem.claim: How to verify Chain-of-Thought reasoning by examining the model’s computational process.

gap.claim: Existing black-box and gray-box verification methods provide limited insight into why a computation fails.

contributions.claim: Introduces Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV), a white-box method that analyzes attribution graphs as execution traces of latent reasoning circuits.
Reports that structural error signatures are highly predictive and domain-specific across reasoning tasks.
Reports using graph-based analysis to guide targeted interventions on individual transcoder features that corrected faulty reasoning.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish CRV as a white-box approach intended to provide scientific insights unavailable through other verification methods, moving beyond error detection toward causal understanding.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that a classifier trained on structural graph features detects a strong signal of reasoning errors.
The authors report that error signatures differ by reasoning domain, indicating distinct computational patterns for different tasks.
The authors report successful correction of faulty reasoning through targeted transcoder-feature interventions guided by their analysis.

narrative_sequence.summary: Existing output- and activation-based verification methods are described as offering limited explanation of computational failures.
The paper introduces CRV, a white-box verification method based on computational-graph analysis.
Attribution graphs for correct and incorrect CoT steps are hypothesized to have different structural fingerprints.
The authors report predictive, domain-specific signatures and intervention-based correction of faulty reasoning.
The authors frame computational-process analysis as a route from detecting errors toward causal understanding.

source_observation.claim: The paper links a proposed structural representation to both predictive error detection and targeted interventions on individual features.

lessons.interpretation: Pairing diagnosis with an intervention test can make a mechanistic claim more informative than prediction alone.
lessons.application: When proposing an internal representation, report whether it supports a targeted manipulation that changes the diagnosed behavior.
lessons.exception: This is unsuitable when the representation lacks identifiable intervention targets or the study only permits observational analysis.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, model details, classifier performance, intervention setup, or quantitative correction rates.
The reported intervention success is not independently verifiable from the abstract alone.
